titles.homePlain: STEP 1 OF 4 · A HOME FOR THE APP

persona.headline: A CLONE OF YOU, WORKING 24/7
persona.body: Scranton Branch turns the CLI agent you already use into a clone of you — one that runs an office of long-running agents and keeps working while you're away. It manages everything around them: context, memory, tasks, triggers, environment, files, and integrations.
persona.ask: FIRST — WHO ARE YOU? (we'll tailor the setup)
persona.technicalDesc: I write code or work in a terminal. Show me CLI commands, flags, and model ids.
persona.nonTechnicalDesc: I'm in marketing, sales, ops, or just starting out. Explain things in plain language.

welcome.headline: YOUR CLONE AND THE FLOOR IT RUNS
welcome.descPlain: Your clone runs a small office of AI workers, and you watch it all from one screen. Here's what's inside:
welcome.desc: Your clone coordinates a hive of AI coding agents — persistent, watchable, all local. Here's what's inside:

engines.label: ELEVEN ENGINES, ONE OFFICE
engines.desc: Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Kimi, Antigravity, Qwen, OpenCode, Crush, pi, Copilot & Cursor — live agents on one floor.
engines.descPlain: Eleven AI assistants — Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Grok and more — working side by side in one shared office.

clone.label: {{godName}} IS YOUR CLONE
clone.desc: Your clone runs the floor — triages requests, routes tasks, and escalates only what needs you.
clone.descPlain: Your clone, {{godName}}, takes your requests, hands work to the right agent, and only interrupts you when it matters.

memory.label: LONG-TERM MEMORY
memory.desc: Each agent keeps notes, mined into a shared, searchable MemPalace.
memory.descPlain: Agents remember what they've done, so they don't start from scratch every time.

commandCenter.label: COMMAND CENTER
commandCenter.desc: Terminal · Floor · Memory · Activity · Tasks · Triggers in one control surface.
commandCenter.descPlain: One dashboard to watch the work, the agents' memory, tasks, and triggers.

guardrails.label: GUARDRAILS
guardrails.desc: Per-agent token budgets, a steer→constrain→stop circuit breaker, and human approvals.
guardrails.descPlain: Spending limits and safety stops keep agents in check — and they can ask you before big actions.

hires.label: READY-MADE HIRES
hires.desc: Grab a pre-configured agent from the Agent Gallery and spawn it in one click.
hires.descPlain: Hire a ready-made agent from the gallery in one click — no setup needed.

home.descPlain: Create a new, empty folder for the app to call home. Everything the app remembers — its own settings and your agents' memory — is stored here. Something like ~/HarnessAgents works well. We'll create it for you if it doesn't exist.
home.desc: Pick a folder where the harness will keep its own files — agent metadata, logs, and any new repos you create from here. Something like ~/HarnessAgents is a fine default. We'll create it if it doesn't exist.
home.notePlain: You won't need to open this folder day-to-day — it's just where the app keeps its notes so nothing is lost when you restart.
home.note: Think of this as the "town hall." The harness pins agent state there so sessions can be picked back up after a restart.

orchestrator.descPlain: {{godName}} is your clone — he reads your requests, breaks them into tasks, and hands them to the right agent. He's the boss of the floor; you're still the boss of him. Choose which AI engine powers him.
orchestrator.desc: {{godName}} is your clone — the boss of the floor you just met. He triages your requests, assigns tasks, and manages the team, while escalating anything that genuinely needs you. Pick the engine and model that power him; give him a longer-context, higher-capability model.
orchestrator.cliAgentPlain: A CLI agent is an AI coding assistant that runs on your computer — popular ones are Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI) and Antigravity (Google Gemini). Your clone is the always-on one that runs your whole office. We recommend Claude Code on Opus 4.8 (1M). You can add or switch the others later.
orchestrator.cliAgent: Each option is a CLI engine (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity/Gemini, or a local proxy like Qwen). Engines marked INSTALLED are already on this machine; INSTALLS ON FIRST RUN means the app sets it up when {{godName}} first starts. Your clone ({{godName}}) is the engine that orchestrates the whole hive. Recommended: Claude Code · Opus 4.8 · 1M. Other providers can be wired per agent later.
orchestrator.workersOnlyHint: Can't drain hive mail yet, so it can't run your clone — still available when hiring workers.
orchestrator.modelNote: This only sets {{godName}}'s engine. You can run other providers per agent later.

repos.descPlain: Add your projects. A project is simply a folder — it can hold code, documents, notes, or any files you want your agents to work with. You can create a brand-new folder or pick an existing one, and add more anytime.
repos.desc: Add the repos you want your agents to work in. Each folder becomes a project (a room on the floor) — multiple agents can share one. You can add more later.

repos.empty: No repos added yet. Optional, but recommended.

permissions.autonomyHead: HOW MUCH CAN AGENTS DO ON THEIR OWN?
permissions.autoLabelPlain: LET AGENTS WORK ON THEIR OWN
permissions.autoOnPlain: On. Agents carry out tasks without stopping to ask — the smoothest experience.
permissions.autoOffPlain: Off. Agents pause and ask you before changing files or running commands.
permissions.autoOn: On. Agents never pause — Claude runs bypassPermissions, Codex bypasses approvals + sandbox, etc.
permissions.autoOff: Off. Each agent asks before edits / shell commands (Claude default, codex -a untrusted, …).
permissions.autoNotePlain: Best when agents work in their own projects. You can change this later, including for individual agents.
permissions.autoNote: The right default for the "control room" experience; a foot-gun on production repos. Override per agent in the Add Agent dialog.
permissions.reliabilityHead: KEEP THINGS RUNNING WHILE YOU'RE AWAY
permissions.reliabilityDescPlain: Your agents keep working on a schedule and in live terminals, even when you step away. These settings keep you in the loop and keep things running.
permissions.reliabilityDesc: Your agents keep working on a schedule and in live terminals. If your computer fully sleeps those timers pause and catch up the moment you're back — nothing is lost, it may just run late.
permissions.keepAwakeDesc: Strong keep-alive: stops your computer from sleeping while an agent is live, so schedules and terminals fire on time even when you step away. Uses more battery — best on power. Off by default.
permissions.notificationsDesc: Get pinged when an agent needs you or a terminal needs reviving — even while you're away. Your system may ask permission the first time one fires.
permissions.openAtLoginDesc: Relaunch the harness after a reboot so scheduled missions resume on their own. No prompt — applies immediately.
permissions.shareStatsDesc: A handful of anonymous events (app opened, agent spawned, feature used) that help improve Scranton Branch — never prompts, code, file paths, or agent output. Full list in TELEMETRY.md; change anytime in Settings.
permissions.stayAwakeDescMac: macOS only lets you set this one yourself. In Battery → Options, turn on "Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off" (on power adapter) so timers keep firing with the display asleep. Without a sleep-preventing setting the Mac still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.
permissions.stayAwakeDescWindows: Windows only lets you set this one yourself. In Settings → System → Power & battery → Screen, blank & sleep, set "On battery power, put my device to sleep" and "When plugged in" to Never (or increase them) so timers keep firing. Without a sleep-preventing setting Windows still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.
permissions.stayAwakeDescLinux: Your desktop environment only lets you set this one yourself. Look for a Power Settings panel (e.g. GNOME Settings → Power, or KDE System Settings → Power Management) and disable automatic sleep/suspend while on power. Without a sleep-preventing setting your machine still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.

caps.guardLimits: "Outside its folders" and "Git" are checked on every command before it runs: file tools, shell commands (including what they pass to bash -c, cmd /c, PowerShell or wsl) and python/node/perl/ruby one-liners. A script saved in a file, or a path the program builds while it runs, cannot be read in advance, so this is a fence for honest mistakes, not a jail. For a hard limit, run the agent in WSL or a container.

conn.step1: Pick a service and get its key
conn.step1Body: Press “Get a key” on the card: it opens the right page at GitHub, Notion, Sentry… Create the key there, paste it into the card and Save. It is stored encrypted on this machine and never shown again.

env.step1Body: NODE_ENV, API_BASE_URL… anything that is not secret. Agents see these in their environment, like any other variable.
env.step2Body: A secret is stored encrypted on this machine and never shown again. A 1Password reference (op://Vault/Item/field) is read from 1Password at the moment it is needed and kept nowhere. Neither goes into an agent’s environment, files or prompt.
env.step3Body: A runner is a command you define (npm test, npm run migrate…) with the secrets it needs. An agent can only ask the app to run it by name: the app runs it in the agent’s worktree and hands back the output with every secret value masked as ***.
env.step4Body: By default a runner asks you before it runs whenever the agent changed files since you last allowed it — the command runs code the agent can edit. APIs and MCP servers that need keys go in Connections instead: the app adds the key to each request.

team.step1Body: Turning Team on gives this office a name and a pair of keys. The keys never leave this machine; teammates only ever see your name.
team.step2: Teams group people, each on its own relay
team.step2Body: Make a team per group you work with (“Barcelona branch”, “Partners”) with “+ New team”. Each team has a relay that passes sealed messages along: a public MQTT broker by default (fast, no daily cap), or an ntfy server (keeps messages 12 h for someone offline; ntfy.sh allows 250 a day per office). A company can run its own relay and put the team on it; one that needs an access token takes it in the team’s Edit form.
team.step3Body: “Invite to …” makes a code that works once, for 24 hours. Send it over a channel you trust (Slack, Signal…). They paste it into “Got an invite?” and both offices appear in that team. You can join other people’s teams the same way, so one office can be in many teams.
team.step4: Decide what each person may do
team.step4Body: Each team sets a default for its members. “May”: Messages lets them write to your orchestrator (View and Manage, to see and run your floor from their office, come next). “Messages”: strict holds every message for you in Inbox → Outside; communication only lets information through and holds requests for action; allow all sends everything straight to your orchestrator. Open a person to give them their own setting instead of the team’s.
team.step5Body: Write from a person’s conversation, or just ask your orchestrator (“tell Barcelona the release moves to Monday”): it writes to them itself, and their replies land in its inbox.
team.step6Body: Every message is encrypted on the sending machine and opened only on the receiving one, and signed so nobody can pose as a teammate. Pairs are post-quantum: each message key also depends on an ML-KEM secret agreed when you paired, so traffic recorded today stays sealed against a future quantum computer. A relay sees a random mailbox name and unreadable bytes. Without a valid invite nobody can get in, even if they know your mailbox. Remove a person or delete a team at any time.

engines.signedInTo: Signed in to: {{list}}. The app’s agents use it.
engines.notSignedInBody: Not signed in with a subscription on this machine. Sign in, or add an API key below.

engines.modelsFound: {{count}} models available: pick one in the field.
engines.saved: Saved. New agents of this engine start with it.
engines.modelHint: Used when you add an agent of this engine without choosing a model. Restart a running agent to change it.
engines.couldNotStart: Could not start {{cmd}}: is it installed?
engines.piSteps: Type /login, press Enter and choose your provider (Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini…). Follow the link it shows. Then press Done.
engines.opencodeSteps: Pick your provider with the arrow keys and Enter, then follow the steps (a link to open, or paste a key). Then press Done.
engines.customBody: Local models (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp) or any OpenAI-compatible server. Every OpenCode and Pi agent gets them; pick a model as provider/model.

engines.customDropped: Saved, without the entries that had no valid name or http(s) URL.
engines.customHint: On a WSL office, localhost is the distribution itself: a server running on Windows needs mirrored networking or the Windows host’s address.
engines.customIdTip: Model ids start with this, e.g. ollama/llama3.1:8b
engines.customKeyStored: key stored — paste a new one to replace it
engines.customKeyPh: API key (optional; local servers usually need none)
engines.customKeyAfterSave: Save first to add a key.
engines.emptyAuth: "{{id}}" has an empty sign-in entry, which hides the key in models.json. Run /logout in the engine and pick {{id}}, then sign in again if you need it.

floors.title: Floors
floors.newHint: Another office, in its own window, with its own orchestrator and agents.
floors.forgetTitle: Forget this floor. Its office folder and the agents’ work are not touched.

boot.title: The office is starting.
boot.body: {{name}} is clocking in; this can take a little while on the first start.

now.sub: What the office is doing, newest first.
now.empty: Nothing has happened yet. When agents work, talk or finish, it shows up here.
now.stoppedCard: Its terminal ended (code {{code}}). Restart it from its page.

god.tip: {{godName}} is the orchestrator (the "god agent"): it reads your requests, hands the work to the right agents, keeps them coordinated and only brings you what needs you.

hivePicker.inUseTitle: Another floor is running this office. Use that window, or pick a different office here.
hivePicker.title: SELECT A HARNESS CONFIG
hivePicker.intro: A harness config is the folder where the app keeps everything for one workspace — its settings, your agents and their memory, tasks, triggers, and history. Each config is separate and self-contained, so you can run different setups side by side. Open the one you were working in, switch to another, or start a new one.
hivePicker.newWhere: NEW CONFIG · WHERE DOES IT RUN?
hivePicker.windowsDesc: Agents run on Windows, in a folder you pick.
hivePicker.wslDesc: Agents, git and tools run inside a Linux distribution.
hivePicker.installWsl: Install it from an administrator PowerShell with wsl --install -d Ubuntu (virtualization must be on in the BIOS), then come back.
hivePicker.name: name

sequential-thinking.desc: Structured step-by-step reasoning scratchpad. No I/O, no secrets.

fetch.desc: Fetch a URL and return its content as markdown (read-only HTTP GET).

filesystem.desc: Read/edit files within the agent workspace only (scoped to cwd at spawn).

git.desc: git in the workspace repo: the Git server and git commands in its shell. Off: the agent cannot run git at all. Applies at once.

github-token.desc: Read/write GitHub issues, PRs, and repos. Requires a personal access token.

GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN.label: Personal access token
GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN.help: A fine-grained token with access to the repos the agents work on (Contents, Issues, Pull requests).

db.desc: Query a Postgres database, read-only. Requires a connection string.

DATABASE_URI.label: Connection string
DATABASE_URI.help: Use a read-only database user. Needs uv (uvx) installed.

search-with-key.desc: Keyed web search. Requires a search-provider API key.

BRAVE_API_KEY.label: API key
BRAVE_API_KEY.help: From the Brave Search API dashboard (the free plan works).

notion.desc: Search, read and edit the Notion pages shared with the integration.

NOTION_TOKEN.label: Integration secret
NOTION_TOKEN.help: Create an internal integration, then share the pages it may use with it (••• → Connections).

sentry.desc: Look up issues, events and releases in Sentry.

SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN.label: User auth token
SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN.help: Scopes: org:read, project:read, project:write, team:read, team:write, event:write.

taskHistory.title: History
taskHistory.empty: Nothing recorded yet. Changes are recorded from now on.

fortress.approveHint: Finish signing in in your browser, including approving this device:
fortress.useIt: Use Fortress for the office browser
fortress.v1Note: Until you sign in, Fortress runs its first-generation engine.
fortress.renewTip: Re-issue the key before it expires
fortress.needsUvWindows: Signing in needs uv for Windows itself (Fortress runs beside the app, not inside WSL): powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

proposal.title: {{agent}} asks for a runner: {{name}}
proposal.note: It runs in {{agent}}'s own folder. The agent only gets the output, with every secret masked, and you are asked again whenever its files changed. You can edit or remove it in Environment.
proposal.newSecretsNote: New secrets are stored encrypted by the app. The agent only ever sees their names.
